 Northeast Ohio food banks confront growing holiday demand after federal SNAP cuts
 Ideastream Public Media | 
 By
 Quinn Schafer 
 Published November 18, 2026 at 4:30 PM EST
 Facebook 
 Twitter 
 LinkedIn 
 Email 
 Abbey Marshall 
 / 
 Ideastream Public Media Many food banks struggle to provide the same nutritional variety that people receiving SNAP benefits can access at a grocery store. 
 Food banks in Northeast Ohio face increased demand this holiday season as communities experience higher costs of living and federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program eligibility has narrowed.
 Northeast Ohio’s 22 counties are served by four regional food banks: Akron-Canton Regional Food Bank, Greater Cleveland Food Bank, Second Harvest Food Bank of North Central Ohio and Second Harvest Food Bank of the Mahoning Valley.
 Kaitie Carver Reed, executive vice president at Akron-Canton Regional Food Bank, said Northeast Ohio was experiencing a surge in need for food assistance even before SNAP eligibility was reduced.
 “We continue to see a high level of demand sustaining in the community,” Reed said. “Last year was the single largest year in the food bank's history. Right now, in 2026, we are experiencing about a 5% increase compared to last year.”
 Jessica Semachko, Greater Cleveland Food Bank’s director of government relations and public education, said the organization has served over 409,000 individuals this year.
 “As food costs increase, gas costs increase, utilities, rent and mortgages,” Semachko said. "That stress on families and seniors on fixed income means that there are less dollars to put food on the table.”
 The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law in July 2025, has led to a significant decrease in SNAP enrollment in Northeast Ohio by expanding work requirements for people over 54, and by removing SNAP access for asylum-seekers and refugees. It also changed work exceptions for veterans, the homeless and former foster youth.
 In the eight counties served by the Akron-Canton Regional Food Bank, Reed said there has been a 12% reduction in SNAP enrollment in 2026 compared to 2025.
 “That is tens of thousands of households across the region that can no longer access SNAP,” Reed said.
 In addition to the people who have lost SNAP support, many eligible people are having trouble enrolling in SNAP because they are confused by the new requirements. Semachko said the Greater Cleveland Food Bank has been working to ensure that eligible community members have the information they need to stay connected to SNAP benefits.
 “We have seen a steady flow of calls seeking out information around (SNAP),” Semachko said. “One of the most important things we have been focused on is to ensure that neighbors know that the SNAP program is operational and that families can continue to apply.”
 Reed said when surveyed, over half of people who use the Akron-Canton Regional Food Bank’s network, many of whom also receive SNAP benefits, said they expect to rely more on the food bank and its network over the next year as they anticipate changes to federal food assistance.
 In a time of financial pressure for families in Northeast Ohio, the holiday season, which comes with colder weather and rising energy bills, can increase strain. 
 Renee Fuller, executive director of Second Harvest Food Bank of the Mahoning Valley, said Second Harvest sees up to double the number of people at some of its pantries during the holidays.
 “We're prepared,” Fuller said. “We know this happens every year as things get a little tougher. We just get stronger and do what we have to do to meet that need, because that's what we're supposed to be doing.”
 Semachko and Reed echoed Fuller’s sentiment that, although demand and costs have risen, Northeast Ohio’s food banks are ready to meet community need this holiday season.
 “We have an amazing network of partners and a fantastic staff that are ready to support people whenever they need us,” Reed said.
 Fuller said in response to growing demand, food banks have to outsource and purchase more food, rather than rely on donations.
 “It’s almost like everything’s on the table,” Fuller said. “Whatever is helpful is something we need to look into or continue to do more of.”
 As costs have increased for families, they have also risen for food banks. Fuller said, with a month and half remining in 2026, Second Harvest Food Bank of the Mahoning Valley has already spent close to what it did last year.
 “We will probably continue to see costs rise as food rises, but we also have transportation costs,” Fuller said. “Fuel surcharges are part of that, and those have almost doubled for us. It’s just crazy how costs just keep going up.”
 But food bank staff say that community partners and donor support has remined strong, helping to meet community need.
 “We experienced such generosity from our community that has allowed us to purchase more fresh produce, more dairy, more nourishing items to feed our community and meet this rising demand,” Reed said.
 Though people can lean on regional food banks for assistance amid federal changes, Semachko said food bank networks can't make up for a change in SNAP benefits.
 “For every one meal a food bank provides, SNAP provides nine,” Semachko said. “To meet the need of the community, we need both strong food banks and a strong federal nutrition program.”
